prompt: In `spread.go`, three workers range over the same channel `jobs`. How many workers receive job 5?
hint: Count how often each number appears across the three lists.

choices.text: All three, and the fastest result is kept
choices.why: Each number appeared once across the lists. A channel gives each value to one receiver.

choices.text: Exactly one
choices.why: Right. A value sent on a channel is received once, by whichever goroutine gets it.

choices.text: Two, so that one can take over if the other fails
choices.why: Nothing in a channel duplicates a value; redundancy would have to be built by hand.

choices.text: w2, because jobs are dealt in turn
choices.why: Nobody deals: in the two runs job 5 went to w1, and the lists did not follow turns.

prompt: Between the two runs of `spread.go`, the jobs each worker took changed. Why?
hint: When does a worker ask for its next job?

choices.text: The channel shuffles values before delivering them
choices.why: A channel delivers in the order values were sent; who receives each one is what varies.

choices.text: Go assigns jobs to workers by a random number
choices.why: No assignment happens; each worker takes the next job when it is free.

choices.text: Each takes the next job when it is free
choices.why: Right. The split follows speed, which is why it is not the same from run to run.

choices.text: The second run had fewer processors
choices.why: Both ran on the same four-processor machine.

prompt: `spread.go` gave three workers 300 ms of work in total. Divided perfectly, how many milliseconds would it take? The run took 120.
A colleague changes `spread.go` so that each worker closes `jobs` when it sees the channel is empty. What goes wrong?
hint: Who knows that sending is over?

choices.text: A later send from `main` panics
choices.why: Right. An empty channel is not a finished one; only the sender knows when it has sent the last job, as lesson 3 put it.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as only one worker closes it
choices.why: Even one early close breaks the next send from `main`.

choices.text: The other workers keep waiting for ever
choices.why: Closing ends every `range` over the channel; waiting is not the failure here.

choices.text: The jobs are done twice
choices.why: A channel still delivers each value once, closed or not.

prompt: `arrival.go` measured `concurrency is not parallelism` and printed `is` first. Why?
hint: A longer word takes longer to measure.

choices.text: Its goroutine was started first
choices.why: `concurrency` was started first, at index 0, and printed third.

choices.text: The channel sorts results by size
choices.why: A channel delivers in the order values were sent, and nothing sorts them.

choices.text: `main` prints the shortest word first
choices.why: `main` prints whatever arrives; it does no comparing.

choices.text: Its job finished first
choices.why: Right. Results arrive in the order the work finished.

prompt: `inplace.go` has four goroutines writing into one slice at the same moment, and `-race` reported nothing. Why is it not a race?
hint: What memory does each goroutine touch?

choices.text: Slices are safe for concurrent use
choices.why: They are not: `append` from several goroutines races, as lesson 16 shows.

choices.text: Each writes only its own element
choices.why: Right, and `main` reads only after `wg.Wait`.

choices.text: The race detector skips slices
choices.why: It watches slice elements like any memory.

choices.text: The writes were too quick to overlap
choices.why: Speed does not make a race safe; separate memory does.

prompt: Results of a fan-out must feed a further stage in the input's order, and the stage reads from a channel. Which fix fits?
hint: One of the two fixes keeps the channel.

choices.text: Write into a slice by index and skip the channel
choices.why: That gives order only once everything is done, and the next stage wants a channel.

choices.text: Use a single worker so results come in order
choices.why: It restores order by giving up the fan-out, which was the point.

choices.text: Carry an index in each result
choices.why: Right. The receiver can put each result back in place and pass them on in order.

choices.text: Add `time.Sleep` so earlier jobs finish first
choices.why: A sleep is timing, not order; lesson 1 showed it promises nothing.

prompt: Several goroutines calling ___ on one shared slice is a race, because they all read and write its length.
hint: The built-in that grows a slice.

prompt: In `firsterr.go`, what does `context.Cause(ctx)` return that `ctx.Err()` does not?

choices.text: How long the context lived
choices.why: Neither reports a duration.

choices.text: The error passed to `cancel(err)`
choices.why: Right: `file 4: checksum mismatch`, where `ctx.Err()` only says `context canceled`.

choices.text: Every error the workers collected
choices.why: That is `errors.Join` of the collected list; the cause is one error, the first.

choices.text: The goroutine that cancelled the context
choices.why: Contexts record no goroutine; the cause is an error value.

prompt: Files 3 and 4 were both damaged, and both errors were printed although the first one cancelled the context. Why was the second not prevented?
hint: When does `check` look at the context?

choices.text: Both files were already being read when the cancel came
choices.why: Right. `check` looks before it starts, so work in flight finishes and its error is kept.

choices.text: `cancel(err)` takes 20 ms to reach other goroutines
choices.why: Cancelling is immediate; the second check had simply started already.

choices.text: `WithCancelCause` ignores the first cancel
choices.why: It is the later calls that change nothing; the first sets the cause.

choices.text: The feeding loop sent file 4 after the cancel
choices.why: Files 1 to 4 went out in the first wave, before any failure.

prompt: Why does a worker in `firsterr.go` skip an error that `errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)` recognises?
hint: Is a cancellation one of the failures being reported?

choices.text: Cancelled errors cannot be joined
choices.why: `errors.Join` accepts any error.

choices.text: To keep the count of clean files right
choices.why: Skipping with `continue` also skips the count; the reason is what the error list should say.

choices.text: It is a consequence of a failure, not one
choices.why: Right. Listing it would bury the damaged files under lines saying `context canceled`.

choices.text: Because `check` returns it as a panic
choices.why: `check` returns `ctx.Err()` as an ordinary error.

prompt: The feeding loop in `firsterr.go` sends with `select { case files <- f: case <-ctx.Done(): break feed }`. What would a plain `files <- f` risk once the workers stop taking files?
hint: Do the workers stop reading the channel after the cancel?

choices.text: A panic, because the context closes `files`
choices.why: A context closes nothing but its own `Done` channel.

choices.text: Nothing here, but it would hand out files nobody checks
choices.why: That is part of it: the workers here still drain the channel, skipping each file, so the loop would feed all twenty for nothing.

choices.text: `main` would sit blocked on its send for ever
choices.why: Right. A send needs a receiver; the `select` gives `main` a way out, the leak lesson 6 described.

choices.text: The files would be sent in the wrong order
choices.why: The loop sends in order either way.

prompt: Put the steps of `firsterr.go` in order, from the first failure to the final report.
hint: The cause is set by the first failure, the list is printed last.
items: a worker's check of a damaged file fails
the feeding loop stops and closes `files`

pairs.right: an index carried in each result

pairs.left: stop the rest at the first failure
tell the workers there is no more work

prompt: Which of these are true of fan-out as `spread.go` builds it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of what the channel guarantees and what it leaves to timing.

choices.text: No job is done twice
choices.why: Yes: each value is received once.

choices.text: Each worker gets the same number of jobs
choices.why: The lists had three, four and five jobs.

choices.text: A faster worker ends up doing more jobs
choices.why: Yes: it comes back to the channel sooner.

choices.text: The results come back in the order the jobs were sent
choices.why: They come back in finishing order, as section 03 showed.

prompt: In the run of `firsterr.go` the lesson quotes, how many of the 20 files were checked cleanly before the first failure stopped the rest?
hint: The first line of the output; other runs printed a different number.

prompt: Three workers shared 300 ms of jobs in `spread.go`, and the run took 120 ms rather than 100. Where did the extra 20 ms come from?
hint: Can the last job be split between two workers?

choices.text: Starting three goroutines costs about 20 ms
choices.why: Starting a goroutine costs far less than a millisecond; lesson 2 measures it.

choices.text: Jobs are indivisible, so some worker finishes last
choices.why: Right. The work cannot be cut into exact thirds, so the run lasts as long as the busiest worker.

choices.text: The mutex around `took` serialised the jobs
choices.why: The lock covers one `append`, a tiny part of each job; the sleeps ran in parallel.

choices.text: The channel is unbuffered, so each send waits 20 ms
choices.why: An unbuffered send waits for a receiver, not for a fixed time.
